name: ivtools
why: X11 vector graphics servers with embedded Tcl interpreters, an old-school environment with an unusual design.

brief.what_it_is: ivtools is a Unix/X11 C++ collection of application frameworks for building custom drawing editors and spatial data servers, bundling a copy of the InterViews 3.1 and Unidraw class libraries with newer libraries for glyphs, graphs, frames and a command interpreter. The README lists 19 executables, including drawtool, idraw, graphdraw, flipbook, comdraw, comterp, glyphterp, drawserv, ivtext, dclock and gclock. The README does not describe concrete inputs and outputs for each program, so the input and output formats are unknown from these pages. The scout note calls it X11 vector graphics servers with embedded Tcl interpreters, but the README never mentions Tcl; it describes a command interpreter (ComTerp) instead.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames ivtools as a layered set of application frameworks for custom drawing editors and generic spatial data applications, preserving and extending InterViews 3.1 and Unidraw. Its fourth layer adds a command interpreter and server mechanism, demonstrated with text, glyph and graphic front-ends.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes four layers: the borrowed InterViews 3.1 libraries and examples, a glyph layer that reuses InterViews light-weight glyph objects, a Unidraw layer (UniIdraw, OverlayUnidraw, TopoFace, GraphUnidraw, FrameUnidraw) for drawing-editor frameworks, and a command layer (ComUtil, Attribute, ComTerp, ComGlyph, ComUnidraw, DrawServ) that adds a command interpreter and server. The README does not say what the command language looks like beyond calling it a command interpreter.

commands_seen.context: From the README's FAQ excerpt on building a stand-alone program on top of ivtools: copy an Imakefile and main.c from an example, modify them, then run ivmkmf -a to generate the Makefile (the command itself is quoted in prose, not shown as a code block).

brief.install_notes: The README says to read the INSTALL file for build instructions, which I did not fetch. It builds with Imake-style tooling (ivmkmf) against X11. The README lists platforms it has built on: SunOS 4.1, Solaris 2.6, Irix 5.2, Linux (Slackware, RedHat, Debian), NetBSD, FreeBSD and Darwin/Mac OS X, with gcc up to 4.3. Windows is supported only through Cygwin (see README.cygwin). Optional third-party pieces: ACE and clippoly (LGPL) are used if configured, and qhull, pstoedit, ghostscript, djpeg and giftopnm are detected at runtime. No accounts or hardware are mentioned. The Homebrew formula's executable list is consistent with the README.
brief.standout: Unlike most drawing tools, it exposes a built-in command interpreter and server mechanism, so a drawing editor can be driven by commands rather than only by a GUI. It also ships the InterViews glyph system (TeX-like light-weight glyphs) and the full Unidraw framework as reusable libraries.
brief.status: Unknown from the evidence I could see. The README is for release 2.1.1 but gives no release date, and I could not check the commit history. The README's platform list and gcc-4.3 and RedHat 7.0 references point to the early 2000s. The ivtools.org documentation URLs returned 404, which suggests the project website has gone stale. Treat it as quiet at best; check the GitHub repo for recent commits before publishing a maintenance claim.
brief.caveats: Old platform list (gcc up to 4.3, RedHat 7.0, Irix 5.2) with no evidence of recent builds. Windows support is only through Cygwin. The README says the HPUX and Alpha configs are out of date. The licence is X11-like permissive, with some bundled third-party code under other terms (LGPL clippoly, the InterViews and TIFF notices). The README's documentation links (ivtools.org doc pages, ivtools-layers.html) returned 404 when I tried them. The INSTALL file was not read. The README names a SourceForge mailing list for questions. The scout note's 'Tcl' claim is not supported by the README.
quotes: ivtools is a layered collection of application frameworks for building custom drawing editors and spatial data servers.
The fourth set adds a command interpreter and server mechanism to ivtools, and demonstrates these capabilities with text, glyph, and graphic front-ends.
It is similar to the X11 copyright, otherwise known as non-copylefted freeware.
